newsitem.title: LEBANON: Reborn MEA aims to fly high again.
newsitem.headline: Reborn MEA aims to fly high again.

text.p: Lebanon's Middle East Airlines, run down and laden with debt after the 1975-90 civil war, is beginning a comeback bid thanks to a $225 million capital injection from the country's central bank.
Chairman Khaled Salam plans to buy aircraft, open new routes and restructure the business.
"The company is being reborn now. I think we will re-emerge very strong. We will be one of the biggest airlines and Lebanon will again be the hub for the whole Middle East," he said.
He told Reuters in a recent interview he expected revenues to rise 10 percent in 1997 from about $300 million in 1996.
MEA is 99-percent owned by the Bank of Lebanon under a $100 million debt-for-equity swap in September that wiped out debts the airline accumulated from 1990 to 1995.
The central bank contributed another $31 million in November and will add $94 million over the next 18 months to complete the $225 million capital increase, Salam said.
However, MEA is still in debt for $20-25 million and its losses in 1996 will be higher than the $38 million in 1996. Salam said he did not foresee a net profit before 1998.
Israel's 17-day blitz on Lebanon in April which cost MEA $12 million in lost revenue, coupled with the rise in international fuel prices and higher salaries caused the 1996 losses, Salam said.
"The year 1997 is the year of challenges because we are pursuing our capital increase programme and moving into a very technologically-sophisticated era," Salam said.
"Losses will grow in 1996, go down in 1997 but 1998 will possibly be a break-even if not a profitable year," he added.
The central bank is banned under its founding law from making commercial investments and this has caused speculation in Beirut that the government wants to privatise MEA quickly.

However, Salam dismissed talk of early privatisation. "Strategically speaking, I am sure the Governor (of the Bank) plans to make MEA profitable because you only sell a profitable company. I think this is his strategy," he said.
Salam said the speed of MEA's recovery would depend on the level of stability in the Middle East.
MEA has 4,130 employees including 186 pilots. Salam said it had cut costs this year by $15 million in Lebanon and $4-5 million in outstations and plans to cut by a further $19-20 million in 1997.
"If everything goes well...we will add another 10 to 12 percent on our revenue in 1997," Salam said.

Part of this should come from a company MEA formed in 1996 with two other firms which signed a 15-year contract to provide catering for MEA and other airlines at Beirut airport. It will start operating in 1997, Salam said.
MEA has also bought American Airlines' Sabre computer technology for airline management and American would train MEA employees on the system in Beirut, Salam said.
"We will be highly-computerised in nine months," he said.
MEA will also bring in foreign consultants as managers in January 1997 for a one- to two-year period.
MEA has so far leased four new Airbuses to add to its 14-plane fleet by May 1997.

"We must work to have at least four more planes either through lease or purchase," Salam added. "This would cost about $200 million. We will get 85 percent from export banks like Eximbank and go to the market for the other 15 percent."
MEA is studying a number of possible new routes including Africa, Bombay, Karachi and eastern Europe and will add two of them in 1997, he added.
